newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook--MTBE keeps gasoline strong.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook--MTBE keeps gasoline strong.

text.p: U.S. spot refined product markets markets east of the Rocky Mountains remain were looking likely to remain strong if somewhat subdued, riding a cresting wave of MTBE strength, traders said Monday.

The MTBE strength was being felt most actutely in New York Harbor, the gateway to gasoline markets in the Northeast, where so much of the fuel burned is reformulated that is blended with the pricey oxygen additive.

While the summertime strength was still in blossom, players were looking on the horizon at factors that may change the market's current tone, including the arrival of gasoline cargoes into the East Coast and more remotely, the upcoming autumn refinery maintenance schedules.

But traders downplayed the impact Iraqi oil may have on refined product markets when it again returns to markets, saying that while underlying futures prices may rise or fall surrounding the news, it will have little effect on the solid demand that underlies this summer's action in product markets.
NEW YORK HARBOR
"MTBE's still in play and looking forward it's still in play," said one gasoline trader. "Octane and RFG are still really strong," he said.

The "A2" regular northern-grade reformulated held its value, with prompt barrels still offered at about 2.25 cents over, and barrels for delivery by the beginning of next month heard offered at 2.00 cents over.

The "V2" and "D2" 93-octane conventional and reformulated northern blends also held their strength, with prompt barrels of both grades offered as high as 7.25 and 11.50 cents over August NYMEX unleaded.

Outnumbered bears in the market were talking up the fixing of both gasoline and MTBE cargoes in Europe, but bullish traders, particularly in the world of MTBE, had a hard time seeing cargoes denting the strength for the next few weeks.
A succession of factors, from production problems to solid demand from refiners and traders of about 300,000 barrels per day, is keeping the market well supported.

"I anticipate this market to continue to be strong through August," said one MTBE trader who pegged prompt spot MTBE in Houston was at 96 cents a gallon and saw holding at around that level over the near-term.
MIDCONTINENT

The outlook this week for gasoline differentials in the Midcontinent was mixed due to conflicting fundamentals. Some traders said fairly good demand amid a slight dip in supply may pressure Group Three values slightly higher.
However, the expected return to full production of National Cooperative Refinery Association's (NCRA) McPherson, Kansas, refinery this week may add to some downward pressure.
The refinery reduced gasoline production last week because of a small fire Monday.
On Monday, Group Three prompt unleaded gasoline differentials were at 0.25 cent to 0.50 cent below the print, about a quarter cent up from Friday because of slightly lower supply.

"We have lower days of supply and futures came off but we do have lots of stuff coming next week in the system," said a trader, adding values should remain stable to slightly higher this week. The system, the Williams Pipeline, has 19-days worth of supply compared to last week's 20-days.
Another trader, however, said differentials could deepen to 1.25 to 1.00 cent under the screen when NCRA returns to full production.

"That would be a pretty cheap range and bring out some good bottom picking," said the trader, noting the average range for the Gruop this time of year is about 0.25 points under to even with the screen.
U.S. GULF

Players said they expected differentials to remain steady this week for conventional unleaded gasoline, which firmed late last week due to healthy demand fueled by Star Enterprises, in what was otherwise a thin market.
"Gulf Coast gasoline is pretty strong. Star Enterprises was a main buyer on Friday, and that pushed the market up. But I'm unsure if they will still be out this week," said one Gulf Coast trader.
On Friday, Star had confirmed it was buying front 22nd cycle M1-grade, adding also that it frequently dipped into the cash market.

News that Iraq will need to sell 1.5 million barrels to 2 million barrels per day of oil in August and the first week o September under the U.N. oil-for-food deal is also unlikely to impact USG differentials.
"Iraq will not do much to change differentials," said a U.S. trader.
On Monday, U.S. Gulf M1-grade was a quarter cent stronger at 0.50 to 0.25 cents under the print.
-- New York Oil Desk 1 212 859 1620
